notes.meaning: God commands Moses to build a square altar out of durable acacia wood, measuring about seven and a half feet on each side and four and a half feet high. This is the main altar for whole burnt offerings, placed in the open courtyard before the tabernacle. It was here that worshippers brought their animals so that sacrifices could be offered to restore peace with God.

differ.view: The bronze altar points directly to Christ Himself, whose divine nature supported the sacrifice of His human nature, rather than picturing the cross or the Lord's Table.
The altar represents the cross as the place of death where Jesus made atonement and where believers must put self to death.

notes.meaning: The four corners of the altar were built with upward-pointing horns carved from the same wood and overlaid with bronze. These horns showed the strength and power of the altar, and the priests smeared the blood of sacrifices upon them. Worshippers could tie sacrificial animals to them, and people in danger sometimes fled to grasp them to seek mercy.

All the tools for the altar had to be made from bronze so they could survive intense heat. These included pots and shovels for clearing away fat-soaked ashes, bowls for catching and sprinkling blood, forks for placing meat on the fire, and pans to carry burning coals. Every tool was set apart solely for holy work around God's dwelling place.

A bronze network grating was placed inside the altar beneath an outer ledge, reaching halfway up its height. This mesh held the burning wood and the sacrifice while letting air circulate underneath and allowing ashes to fall through. Four bronze rings were attached at its corners so the whole altar could be carried securely.

Poles made of acacia wood and covered in bronze were slid into the rings along the sides of the altar. These poles allowed the Levites to lift and transport the holy altar without touching it with their hands. They ensured that God's people could take the place of sacrifice with them wherever they traveled in the wilderness.

The altar was to be built hollow out of wooden boards, following the exact pattern shown to Moses on Mount Sinai. Making it hollow kept it light enough to carry on long journeys across the desert. When set up in camp, the inside was likely filled with earth or unhewn stones to serve as a hearth for the fire.

differ.view: The altar was kept completely hollow as a picture of Christ emptying Himself when He became human, rejecting the idea that it was ever filled with earth.

notes.meaning: God orders an open courtyard to be set up around the tabernacle tent, starting with curtains on the south side. These curtains were made of fine white linen, stretching about one hundred and fifty feet in length. They marked out a boundary between the everyday world and the sacred space where God lived with His people.

The long curtains on both the south and north sides were hung on twenty wooden posts resting in solid bronze bases. Silver hooks and silver connecting rods held the linen walls firmly in place along each wall of one hundred cubits. The bright silver bands and white linen reminded worshippers of the holiness required to enter God's presence.

The back of the courtyard on the west side and the front on the east side were each fifty cubits wide, which is about seventy-five feet across. Ten posts set in ten bronze bases supported the western wall behind the tabernacle tent. The eastern wall faced the rising sun and contained the only entrance into the sacred area.

On the east side, white linen curtains ran fifteen cubits out from each corner toward the center, leaving space for a gate between them. Each of these side curtains was supported by three posts set in three bronze bases. This created two equal wings of fabric that framed the open entryway into the court.

The center gate of the courtyard was thirty feet wide and hung with a colorful curtain of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen. Supported by four posts in bronze bases, this bright gate was far richer in appearance than the plain white curtains beside it. It was the single, wide way for any Israelite to bring their offerings and enter God's presence.

The completed courtyard formed a rectangle one hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide, surrounded by walls seven and a half feet high. Every pillar around the perimeter had a bronze base at the ground and silver hooks and bands at the top. Because the tabernacle tent stood taller than these linen walls, people outside the court could still see the sacred tent rising above them.

All the tools and tent pegs used to set up the tabernacle tent and the courtyard had to be made of sturdy bronze. These metal stakes were driven into the soil and tied with cords to keep the posts upright in desert winds. While gold and silver were used inside God's tent, bronze was used for the tough work outside.

The people of Israel were commanded to supply the finest olive oil, produced by gently crushing olives rather than grinding them in a mill. This clear, slow-burning oil kept the golden lampstand shining brightly without foul smoke. The pure fuel serves as a picture of the Holy Spirit, who fills believers so their lives shine with God's light before others.

Aaron and his sons were instructed to care for the lamps inside the Holy Place, outside the veil that concealed the Ark of the Covenant. They were to trim the wicks, add oil, and keep the light shining before the Lord from dusk until dawn as an enduring law for all generations. This regular service was a shadow of Christ's ministers faithfully sharing the light of God's Word with His people.

differ.view: The command to keep the lamps burning continually meant they were tended so they burned faithfully day and night without ever going out.
The phrase continually meant the lamps were lit every evening and put out each morning, since the tabernacle had natural daylight through the front curtain.
